title: Adaptive Deployment Fabric — POC Design Notes and Recommendation
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures a lightweight POC design for an Adaptive Deployment Fabric (ADF) that lets us evaluate hosted, dedicated, and private deployment topologies under a single routing and policy abstraction. The goal is to produce a repeatable patterns cookbook and a small POC implementation that customers can trial during a 6‑week engagement.

Context and motivation:
- Customers increasingly ask for: predictable latency for critical routes, cost-efficient fallbacks, and data-sovereignty guarantees per tenant/route.
- Historically we present three distinct options (hosted / dedicated / private). The ADF POC combines those options with a control-plane policy layer so a single integration can flex between venues without code changes.
- Target audience for the POC: mid-market to enterprise customers with mixed sensitivity data, e.g., fintech and healthcare POCs that want both regional/hosted speed and private on-prem inference for sensitive flows.

High-level goals for POC:
- Demonstrate a routing fabric that can: route by tenant, route by route, and route by tokenized SLO profiles (latency-first, cost-first, sovereign-only).
- Validate fallback behaviors when preferred capacity is saturated (e.g., move to quantized model on hosted or to dedicated pool).
- Surface cost delta and latency tail impact for at least three representative workloads: chat (short dialog), summarization (long inputs), and embeddings (batch).
- Produce a canonical integration pattern + rollout checklist for customers.

Assumptions and constraints:
- Prototype uses existing Redwood runtime binaries; no low-level kernel changes.
- POC infra: combination of hosted region (us-west), a small Dedicated pool (4x A100 equivalent), and a private VM cluster simulated in GCP with VPC peering.
- Use an open 7B model family with two variants: base FP16 and quantized 4-bit.

ADF logical components (conceptual):
1) Policy Plane (control plane): stores routing rules, data sovereignty labels, SLO profile per route, and model variant preferences. Exposes CRUD and evaluated policy decisions via REST.
2) Router / Decision Agent (request path): evaluates policy with a short-circuit cache and emits a placement decision (hosted/dedicated/private + model variant + routing metadata).
3) Telemetry & Cost Estimator: real-time token cost model plus latency probe collector; provides hints to the policy plane for automated routing updates.
4) Execution adapters: light shims that translate placement decisions into calls to Redwood hosted API, dedicated endpoint pool, or private deployment endpoint.

Design patterns to validate in POC:
- Route affinity: stable mapping of tenant -> placement to maintain cache-warmth and KV reuse while allowing policy changes at off-peak times.
- Priority fallback chain: e.g., private -> dedicated -> hosted-quantized -> hosted-base (with rate/latency thresholds).
- Per-route SLO hedging: for latency-sensitive routes issue parallel fast (smaller model) + slow (larger model) calls and prefer first good answer if within quality thresholds.
- Cost-aware gradual shift: telemetry informs policy to move low-QPS routes from hosted FP16 to hosted-quantized to save cost.

Example placement rules (POC sample):
- "payments-ocr" route: sovereign=true, preferred=private, fallback=dedicated, enforced: do-not-fallback-to-hosted.
- "email-assist" route: sovereign=false, preferred=dedicated(low-latency), cost-window: move to hosted-quantized if 72h running cost > 3x threshold.
- "search-embeddings" route: batch-friendly; prefer hosted embeddings with batching adapter; use dedicated for SLA-critical queries.

Data, security, and audit model:
- Tagging at the request level: each request carries a compact label set (tenant-id, route-id, data-class). Router uses tags to evaluate policy.
- Audit log: immutable placement events (request id, placement decision, reason code) stored in S3/GCS for customer review.
- Private deployments: simulated KMS integration (customer key) and no telemetry exported outside customer network; control plane only stores policy hashes and non-sensitive telemetry.

Operational SLOs & metrics to collect during POC:
- 99th token latency per route (hosted / dedicated / private).
- Per-request cost estimate and realized cost per 24h window.
- Cache-hit ratio for prefix/KV cache when affinity maintained.
- Fallback frequency and average cost delta per fallback.

Failure modes and mitigation:
- Capacity saturation: router should surface requeuing or rate-limit decisions with graceful 429 and diagnostic payload. Plan to validate with load tests that force fallback chain.
- Inconsistent model outputs across variants: need a simple regression test harness (prompt set with semantics checks) to block auto-fallbacks that would reduce quality beyond threshold.
- Control-plane unavailability: decision-agent has a local read-only cache of policy; fallback to simple heuristic (prefer local dedicated pool) if cache stale > 30s.

POC success criteria (measurable):
- Demonstrate end-to-end routing for three routes with at least two placement transitions exercised (e.g., private->dedicated, dedicated->hosted-quantized).
- Telemetry must produce cost and latency correlations; cost savings signal for quantized variant >= 30% for embeddings workload.
- Can reproduce a simulated region outage and observe automatic failover with <5s decision latency and <1% error rate on requests retried.
- Regression guard prevents dangerous fallback in at least 90% of tested prompt set cases.

Week-by-week POC plan (6 weeks):
- Week 0: Kickoff + environment provisioning + prompt set collection with customer.
- Week 1: Implement policy plane prototype + simple router agent and adapter to hosted API.
- Week 2: Wire dedicated pool and private simulated endpoint; basic telemetry ingestion.
- Week 3: Implement fallback chains, run directed load tests, collect baseline metrics.
- Week 4: Integrate regression guard + canary rules; evaluate quality delta across model variants.
- Week 5: Run sovereignty scenarios and region outage drills; refine policies and HA behavior.
- Week 6: Customer walkthrough, handoff doc, and next-steps recommendations.

Rollout checklist / customer artifacts to deliver:
- Pocket guide: "How to map routes to ADF policies" (1–2 pages).
- Example policy templates for common archetypes (low-latency, sovereign, cost-optimized).
- Integration snippets (router agent + adapter) for Node/Python SDKs.
- Post-POC runbook: how to convert a POC policy to production policy with audit and SLA controls.

Open questions and risks to surface early:
- To what extent can we safely quantize (quality vs cost) across customer prompt sets? Need customer-provided prompts and quality SLO targets.
- Private deployment telemetry: what exact artifacts can leave the private network? We need legal signoff for telemetry opt-ins.
- Operational cost visibility: how granular must cost signals be to drive automated routing decisions without oscillation?

Appendix: quick decision matrix (example)
- Criteria: Latency tail, Data sensitivity, QPS burstiness, Cost-sensitivity -> Recommended placement (private/dedicated/hosted-quantized/hosted-base).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally lightweight and implementation-centric. The POC is meant to prove the policy + routing abstraction more than to build a feature-complete control plane.
- Feedback requested from runtime team on: (1) feasible caches to maintain affinity without leaking tenant data, (2) quick probes we can use to estimate tail latency for each pool.
- Feedback requested from product: which customer archetypes should we prioritize templates for in week 0?

Contact and next step owners:
- POC lead: Marcus Hale (owner).
- Runtime integration: Tom Becker.
- Telemetry and cost modeling: Rina Solis.
